column3: The immediately preceding counterfactual wish for guidance sets up the next wish for another turn after punishment is seen.
Prior neglect and an unbreakable pledge leave the elder unable to depart, paralleling the focus's too-late wish to alter a settled result.
It states that ihsan receives ihsan, clarifying the good-doer status the speaker wishes to have attained.
It closely parallels the wish for another return, but frames the hoped-for changed identity as becoming believers.
Its assurance against despair supplies the merciful opening available before the belated wish in the focus.
The divine creative command does not clarify the human wish to return and act well after seeing punishment.
Lot's conditional wish for strength or protection shares a frustrated counterfactual form but has a distinct crisis.
The immediately preceding regret over neglect is the first of the escalating belated speeches completed by the focus verse.
The description of beautiful women does not clarify ihsan as the desired moral identity.
Followers in the Fire wish for another turn to disavow their leaders, a close but already less direct post-judgment return wish.
It links striving with divine guidance and God's companionship with the muhsinin, supplying a positive path absent from the speaker's past.
The loss of all help after collapse gives a limited image of a condition that cannot be reversed by wishing.
The terrified are seized without escape, concretizing the inescapable moment in which the focus speaker sees punishment.
It commands return and submission before punishment arrives, directly contrasting the focus's request only after it is seen.
It warns against professing to hear while refusing real reception, a pattern that helps explain a later regretful claim.
The formula for recompensing the muhsinin clarifies the positive standing the focus speaker belatedly seeks.
It gives ihsan concrete ethical content as answering harm with what is better, rather than merely naming the desired identity.
Its recompense of the muhsinin supports the desired identity but adds little after the more direct reward formulations.
God seeing the messenger stand does not develop the focus's human seeing of punishment or return wish.
It commands following the best revelation before punishment comes suddenly, directly marking the action foregone in the focus.
The deniers call resurrection a losing return, whereas the focus asks for a voluntary return to change conduct.
The repeated recompense formula adds little beyond earlier verses explaining the reward of the muhsinin.
It shows evil earnings striking their makers, supplying the causal consequence that precedes the focus's sight of punishment.
It says each person's striving will be seen, clarifying why a wish for a new, good course arises when consequences become visible.
Another repeated recompense of the muhsinin offers little new clarification of the desired status.
A historical military restoration called a return does not illuminate the eschatological wish for another moral opportunity.
Self-sufficiency names an interior posture that can prevent the responsive conduct the focus speaker later wishes to have had.
The warning against fabricated prophetic speech does not clarify a condemned person's counterfactual request.
It is the direct divine answer: signs had already come, but were denied arrogantly, explaining why the requested return is too late.
God's nearness to the God-conscious and muhsinin gives the desired identity a present relational significance.
The recurring recompense formula is redundant with the earlier reward verses for the muhsinin.
The trumpet and universal rising locate the final reconstitution after which a person cannot choose a new earthly turn.
It contrasts the good response of the God-conscious with the focus speaker's delayed wish to have been among good-doers.
The repeated return of sight concerns failed cosmic inspection, not an opportunity to return and act well.
The dispute of the condemned assembly supplies only broad infernal context for the focus's individual wish.
The confirming Book warns wrongdoers while bringing good news to muhsinin, setting the two alternatives before final punishment.
Being perceived as a benefactor in a plea for a prisoner does not clarify the focus's eschatological moral identity.
God's taking and retaining of souls marks the death-boundary beyond which the requested voluntary return is unavailable.
The prayer joins worldly and final good with protection from Fire, expressing the preventive good the focus speaker seeks too late.
It anticipates a counterfactual excuse for lacking revelation, then answers that clear guidance came and was denied, closely matching the focus's sequence.
The condemned confess manifest error, a direct infernal acknowledgment that parallels the focus's belated recognition.
The recurring question about punishment and warnings connects experienced punishment to earlier warnings that were not heeded.
It contrasts a worldly punishment with the greater punishment of the Hereafter, sharpening the focus's final warning horizon.
The night worshipper fears the Hereafter and hopes for mercy, providing the opposite present orientation to the focus's delayed request.
It promises the best recompense for believers who do good, clarifying what being among the muhsinin would have meant before judgment.
Those who resisted the messenger will know, when they see punishment, who was farthest astray, closely echoing the focus's moment of sight.
The condemned attribute their misguidance to criminals, adding an infernal confession that complements the focus speaker's wish to revise conduct.
The direct presentation of the promised Hell supplies the object whose sight triggers the focus's counterfactual plea.
Standing before the Lord, admitting the truth, and being told to taste punishment closely depicts the scene behind the focus's sight of torment.
The fire's total enclosure and the command to fear God give concrete preventive force to the focus's warning.
The hypothetical claim that a prior reminder would have produced sincere service parallels a too-late counterfactual appeal.
It says unbelievers would act differently if they knew the moment they cannot ward off the Fire, directly clarifying the focus's late realization.
It promises present good and unbounded reward for those who do good, supplying the positive alternative to the focus speaker's lost opportunity.
The garden recipients receive their Lord's gift because they had been muhsinin beforehand, contrasting prior conduct with belated aspiration.
A mistaken expectation that humans and jinn would not lie about God does not clarify return, punishment, or ihsan.
It announces the evil final return of the tyrannical, framing the destination the focus speaker sees.
The denial of resurrection identifies an earlier stance that leaves people unprepared for the scene in the focus.
The question whether any remnant remains offers only a broad image of irreversible divine destruction.
It joins personal accountability, return to God, and disclosure of deeds, supplying the judgment framework for the focus's plea.
Submission to God joined with ihsan receives reward and freedom from fear, defining the state the speaker wishes to have reached.
The promise of angelic military support to believers does not clarify the focus's return wish or moral reversal.
Joseph's prayer to die submitted and join the righteous offers a distinct positive endpoint, but not another opportunity after punishment.
The messenger is presented as an excellent model for those hoping in God and the Last Day, giving ihsan an embodied pre-judgment form.
It connects wrongful allegiance with God's displeasure and enduring punishment, a route into the consequence seen in the focus.
Creation from one self and divine lordship do not clarify the focus's belated request for a return.
Jonah's prior glorification averts a prolonged consequence, offering a limited contrast of timely conduct before an irreversible outcome.
Abraham's request for righteous offspring does not illuminate the focus's request for another personal turn.
Turning away from revealed judgment is linked to being struck for some sins, illustrating a prior refusal with consequences.
It promises the best reward and more to those who do good, clarifying the final outcome associated with ihsan.
God's establishing truth by His words does not clarify the focus's individual counterfactual or moral aspiration.
The water and vegetation cycle ends in reflection but does not materially clarify the return wish or final punishment.
The creative command concerns divine power, not a human being's lost chance to return and do good.
The leveled earth after upheaval does not add to the focus's request for another turn.
The messenger's duty to deliver and God's duty to account supplies only a broad judgment framework.
Abraham's model of disavowal and return to God gives a distant voluntary-response contrast to the focus's late plea.
Resistance to God's completed light is a broad instance of rejection, but does not develop the return or punishment scene.
Job's complaint of affliction and suffering does not clarify eschatological punishment or a request to return.
The exemplary stance and warning against turning away offer only a general contrast to the focus speaker's prior refusal.
Moses' request to ease his task does not clarify a second chance after final punishment.
It traces faith, God-consciousness, and ihsan as a sustained path loved by God, concretizing the conduct desired in the focus.
Those who want revelation replaced are answered with the messenger's fear of a great-day punishment, linking rejection of guidance to the feared outcome.
Lot's offer in response to his people's demand does not illuminate the focus's moral return wish.
The law of testimony at approaching death does not clarify post-punishment return or becoming a good-doer.
It directly commands ihsan and says God loves the muhsinin, giving practical present content to the identity named in the focus.
Moses' request for a minister from his family does not clarify the focus's eschatological request.
The command to dispute in the best manner gives a limited ethical instance of ihsan, but not the focus's judgment setting.
Thamud are given enjoyment only until a fixed time, underscoring a warning period that ends before punishment arrives.
The good loan's multiplied return and final return to God offer a distant reward-based account of good action.
Solomon's search for the hoopoe does not clarify the focus's seeing of punishment or desired return.
Its command to justice and ihsan directly defines the moral practice the focus speaker wishes to have undertaken.
The people's indifference to warning illustrates the earlier refusal whose consequences make a later plea futile.
God erases the worst deeds and rewards by the best deeds, clarifying the evaluative horizon of the wished-for ihsan.
Extended worldly enjoyment gives only a general delay-before-consequence frame.
Revelation placed on the messenger's heart to make him a warner supplies only the upstream warning function.
Jesus' signs are stated as evidence for believers, a broad reminder that signs call for response before judgment.
The mountains' dissolution supplies a final-day image but does not clarify the speaker's request for another turn.
On recognizing a mistaken appearance, the queen immediately confesses wrongdoing and submits, contrasting timely correction with the focus's belated appeal.
Jonah's losing lot does not clarify a final punishment scene or the desire to become among good-doers.
Even an overwhelming visible sign would not move the deniers, sharpening why mere sight of punishment cannot create a usable new response.
Returning a greeting with what is better gives a narrow ethical instance of acting better, without the focus's judgment context.
When the final fulfillment comes, those who neglected it ask to be returned so they can act differently, closely matching the focus's belated counterfactual.
At the Fire, deniers wish to be returned so they will not deny their Lord's signs and will become believers, a close parallel to the focus's plea.
It denies the validity of repentance only when death confronts a person, directly establishing the too-late boundary in the focus.
Those surprised by the Hour express regret while bearing their burdens, providing the sudden final recognition behind the focus's wish.
It challenges whether belief will come only after the punishment has fallen, clarifying the futility of response after direct sight.
Pharaoh declares belief only when drowning overtakes him, a narrative instance of confession under irreversible punishment.
Wrongdoers ask for a short delay so they can answer the call, a related late request for time to change their response.
At death, the wrongdoer asks to be returned so that he may do righteousness in what he left behind, nearly restating the focus's wish.
It directly refuses the requested return and places a barrier until resurrection, making explicit the closure assumed by the focus.
The wrongdoer regrets on the Day and wishes he had taken a way with the messenger, identifying a lost path before judgment.
The regret identifies Satan's diversion from the remembrance after it came, supplying a cause for the later remorse.
The sinners say they have now seen and heard and ask to be returned to do righteousness, one of the closest parallels to the focus.
The command to taste punishment for forgetting the meeting of this Day makes the connection between prior neglect and final consequence explicit.
The people of Hell ask to be taken out so they can do righteousness unlike their former deeds, directly parallel to the desired second chance.
Its blackened faces and abode for the arrogant immediately continue the focus's divine reply, identifying the final consequence of the arrogance named in 39:59.
The condemned are told that their rejection when called to faith was greater than their present self-hatred, explaining post-judgment remorse through prior refusal.
The condemned acknowledge the two deaths and lives and ask for a way out, a related plea made only after full recognition.
The inhabitants of the Fire ask its guardians to lessen punishment for one day, another constrained appeal after the consequence has arrived.
The guardians answer that clear messengers had already come, directly connecting a late plea in Hell to previously available guidance.
On seeing punishment, wrongdoers ask whether there is any way back, directly echoing the focus's request for another turn.
The condemned are told they are forgotten because they treated this meeting as forgettable and were deceived by worldly life, clarifying the antecedent neglect.
A person facing death asks for a brief delay to give charity and become righteous, a pre-death counterpart to the focus's too-late request.
The people of the Blaze admit that listening or reasoning would have kept them from it, directly framing the missed response before final punishment.
Their confession of sin after the warning has become punishment supplements the focus's belated realization.
On the near Day, the wrongdoer wishes he were dust, a final-state expression of regret that contrasts with the focus's wish to act differently.
When Hell is brought near, the human being remembers but recognizes that remembrance is then of no use, closely supporting the focus's timing.
